full_judgment:
As such, the sponsors of a company availing EEF are required to purchase the shares issued in the name of the GoB within a period of 8 years from the date of first disbursement. The purpose of such stipulation is that by such purchase of shares by the sponsors the GoB shall be able to recover its investments and put such returned investment to use in financing other eligible projects. Further, EEF Circular No. 28 dated 4-12-2008 and the clarification letter No. EEF/ 1/Pa/Krishi/2014-346 dated 9-7-2014 thereto issued by the pro-forma respondent No. 5 sets out further guidelines for purchase of the shares of the GoB by the sponsors of the companies in case of agro based projects as follows: 

 That in the year 2009,. the pro-forma respondent No.5 entered into a Sub-Agency Agreement dated 1-6-2009 with ICB through which all operational activities in relation to the EEF were handed over to ICB including the functions previously performed by the evaluating institutions as per the conditions stated in EEF Circular Nos. 6 and 7. Pursuant to the said Sub-Agency Agreement the pro-forma respondent No.5 issued EEF Circular Nos. 29 and 32 dated 16-7-2009 and 12-8-2010 respectively detailing the responsibilities and the activities to be conducted by 1CB in relation to the EEF henceforth (Annexure-"D", "D(1)" & "D(2)"); that, moreover in pursuance of the transfer of operational activities in relation to the EEF to ICB in 2009, ICB has been granted a General Power of Attorney dated 30-3-2017 by the GoB with powers to inter alia initiate legal action in relation to the EEF and to swear affidavit in relation to any cases in relation to the EEF. As such, the GoB as shareholder in the respondent No.1 Company has filed the instant application represented by ICB (Annexure-"E"); as per the guidelines set out in the said EEF Circulars and following appraisal by the pro-forma respondent No.7 of an application for availing EEF, the pro-forma respondent No. 5 by its letter No. EEF/38(117)/2004-944 dated 01.08.2004 sanctioned an EEF equity investment of Taka 3,80,00,000 (Taka three crore eighty lac only) in favor of the respondent No. 1 Company on the terms and conditions inter alia that the equity participation of the GoB in the respondent No. 1 Company shall not exceed 49% of the paid up capital of the respondent No.1 Company (Annexure- "F"); that as per the requirements of the said EEF Circulars and pursuant to the said sanction letter an Investment Agreement dated 29-9-2004 was entered into between the Company and the pro-forma respondent No. 7 acting on behalf of the pro-forma respondent No.5 and the 3,80,000 shares in the respondent No. 1 Company of Taka 3,80,00,000 (Taka three crore eighty lac only) in value were issued in the name of the "Government of the Peoples Republic of Bangladesh, EEF Unit, Bangladesh Bank" representing the equity stake of the GoB in the respondent No. 1 Company and held in the custody of the pro-forma respondent No.7. Clause No. 5 of the said Investment Agreement contains stipulations to the effect that the respondent Nos. 2-3 being the sponsors of the respondent No.1 Company shall purchase the shares of the GoB within 8 (eight) years of the date of first disbursement (Annexure-"G"); that the conditions relating to purchase of shares of the GoB by the sponsors under the said Investment Agreement are similar to and reflect the requirements of EEF Circular Nos. 6 and 7. Moreover, such stipulation as to purchase of the shares of the GoB within 8 years of the first disbursement of the EEF has also been incorporated into Article 49 of the Articles of Association of the respondent No.1 Company. Mr Atiar Rahman Ansary of the pro-forma respondent No. 7 is acting as a nominated director on the board of the respondent No. 1 Company representing the interest of the GoB. The shareholding structure of the respondent No.3 Company as evident from the Form-XII dated 12-2-2004 and Form-XV dated 30-10-2004 is as follows: 

 4. Learned Advocate Mr Provir Neogi, alongwith Mr Mehran Morshed, appeared for the petitioner and, having placed the petition as well as Affidavit-in-Reply alongwith the documentary evidence annexed therewith, they submit that, admittedly, since 2008, when the substratum gone, the company is not in operation. Therefore, the substratum of the company has gone and the Company is liable to be wound up. In support of his contention, the learned Advocates for the petitioner has referred to 11 BLD (AD) 171 = 43 DLR (AD) 164. The learned Advocates for the petitioner also submit that, if the equity investment of Taka 3.40 crore be converted into the loan, as prayed for by the sponsors, then also the petitioner will have remedy under section 241 and that the availability of relief in the Artha Rin Court is no bar to proceed under section 241 of the Act. Next, referring to a case reported in 55 DLR 478: Amir Hossain vs Homeland Footwear Ltd, he continues that, it has been held in that case, that, if the requirements of section 241 of the Act is satisfied the company is liable to be wound up, even if there are other equally efficacious remedy. They also submit that, similar view, as that of 55 DLR 478, has been taken in another case referred in 17 DLR (SC) 52: Ladli Prashad vs Karnal Distillery Co. Ltd. The learned: Advocates empathically submits that, when the company itself has no prospect to continue as a going concern, therefore, the conversion of the aforesaid amount of equity investment into loan, will not in any way improve the situation. Moreover, it is within the desertion of Bangladesh Bank, they continue, to decide whether they will convert the equity amount, invested in the respondent No.1, into loan. Therefore, they prayed for winding up of this company and to appoint an Official Liquidator accordingly. 

 5. Learned Advocate Mr ASM Shahariar Kabir alongwith Ms. Shamima Akhter appeared for the respondent Nos.1-3 and submit that, on 15-6-2004 MIDAS Financial Limited had sent a project profile to the Bangladesh Bank for approval of the project of the respondent No.1 company (for the purpose of granting EEF) and Bangladesh Bank had, accordingly, approved the said project and had also sanctioned a limit of Tk. 3.8 crore in favour of MIDAS Financing Limited, vide its sanction letter No. EEF/38(117)/2004-944, dated 1-8-2004: Annexure-F, for buying 49% shares in the respondent No.1 Company and that there was a condition, in clause No.6 of the said sanction letter, that, "এছাড়াও সরকারের নামে ইস্যুকৃত শেয়ার সমূহ বাংলাদেশ ব্যাংক আট (৮) বৎসর সমাপনান্তে বিক্রয় করতে না পারলে উক্ত শেয়ারগুলো মূল্যকে উদ্যোক্তার নামে ঋনে রুপান্তর করা হবে।” The learned Advocate further submits that, pursuant to the said sanction letter, vide Memo No. EEF/38/(117)/2004-944, dated 1-8-2004 (Annexure-F), the respondent No.1 Company entered into an agreement on 29-9-2004 and, pursuant to the said agreement, MIDAS has purchased 3,80,000 (three lac eighty thousand) shares and their representative have become nominee directors in respondent No.1 Company, as representative of Bangladesh Bank. He also submits that, thereafter, MIDAS has disbursed in total Taka 3.40 crore, between on 5-6-2005 to 22-8-2006. But they did not disburse Taka 40,00,000 (forty lac), as promised in the said agreement. Learned Advocate next referred to Article No. 49 of the Article of Association (AoA) of the respondent No.1 Company and submits that, in compliance with the said agreement, provisions has been made in the Article 49 that, if the 49% shares cannot be bought backs, then at the end of eight years, Bangladesh Bank will have authority to convert those shares into debt of the sponsors and Bangladesh Bank will also fix up the interest for such debt. The learned Advocate has also referred a recent circular of Bangladesh Bank i.e. EEF circular No. 14, dated 29-10-2003, wherein, Bangladesh Bank has also stipulated that, if the Government shares in any company, that has availed equity fund under EEF scheme, cannot be sold within eight years (to refund the Government's investment), then Bangladesh Bank can convert the said equity investment figure into loan. The learned Advocate also submits that, the respondent No.1 company, on 10-10-2017, has requested the Bangladesh Bank to convert the EEF fund into loan. On the same date (on 10-10-2017) the respondent No.3 made another application with similar prayer to MIDAS, but MIDAS has not attended to that request and had referred the matter to Bangladesh Bank. Bangladesh Bank, vide, a letter dated 24-10-2017 has declined to consider the request, by taking the excuse that the matter was sub-judice, although it had authority to convert the equity fund into loan, he submits. The learned Advocate mainly contends that, the promoters have invested 51% equity in the company and the company is in a position to survive in the competition and to overcome the difficulties that it was facing. Now, he submits, if at this stage, the company is ordered to be wound up then the entire investment made by the sponsor-shareholders of the company will become a total loss. Learned Advocate next submits that, if the EEF equity is converted into loan then the petitioner will suffer no loss, rather it will help survival of the company, and the Company is commercially viable. But, Bangladesh Bank, without considering the application of the petitioner, to convert their equity into loan, has rejected to the same, mechanically, and on lame excuse, he asserts. Therefore, the learned Advocate for the respondents prayed that the petition for winding up may be rejected and that the equity fund be converted into loan, for which the company shall provide proper security and shall also pay applicable interest at the similar rate as may be fixed by Bangladesh Bank in respect of the similar nature of project. The learned Advocate also referred to the Affidavit-in-reply, filed against the affidavit-in-opposition, and further submits, referring to the Affidavit-in-Opposition (Annexure-3 series), that out of 518 agro projects, only 33 has partly bought back their shares (held in the name of EEF) and no other projects could bought back their shares. Therefore, instead of filing of wholesale applications for winding up, Bangladesh Bank may be directed to convert the equity fund into loan, more so, when the Bangladesh Bank/MIDAS could not provide or had failed to provide, Taka 40,000,00 (forty lac) as it had agreed to Bangladesh Bank/MIDAS has contributed to the temporary sickness of the project, he also submits. Therefore, he occludes by stating that, this case should not attract the mischief under section 241 to reward the petitioner for their own default. 

 8. Facts are almost undisputed except that, the respondent claimed that, if the company is not wound up it has every possibility to survive and the investor has raised and invested a huge amount of money required for such project and scheme and that, if the equity fund (EEF) is converted into loan the project can survive and grow. However, the petitioners opposed this proposition, insisting that the Company is no more in going concern and had lost it's substrata, so this is a fit case for winding up of the Company. 

 9. The decisions submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioner, noted herein above, cannot be differed form and, these have not only laid down the sound principles of law, but are binding on this Division too. But, the facts and circumstances under which those decisions were given are different from the instant matter, while quite different and new issues have come up for decision in this case. Therefore, the case cited is liable to be distinguished from the present one. 

 10. In this case, I find that the sponsors are very much eager to try their best to help survive the company and in overcoming the difficulties. Besides, they are basing their claim upon the agreed terms that leaves scope for conversion of EEF equity fund into loan. Besides, the sponsors have made application to MIDAS and Bangladesh Bank to convert the equity fund into loan, who ought to have taken the same for consideration. They could have accepted the proposal or could not have accepted the same, but, they have kept this matter suspended, because this matter was sub-judice. 

 11. It may be pertinent to mention here, that the Bankruptcy Act, 1997, provides for reorganization scheme and the scheme for reconstruction. Therefore, in all appropriate cases, where the directors or the company make an approach to the lender, or to the equity investor, as I find in the present case, they shall, in my considered view, first of all make or cause to be made, a fresh feasibility study of a sick or nearly sick project, to assess and understand for themselves, if it would be feasible to go for a reorganization scheme, resorting to the mechanism and procedure as prescribed by law, may be under a different name and within the scheme of the applicable law, by maintaining the spirit of the Bankruptcy Act. 1997 (in the sanction advice). Of course this should not be done or considered as a matter of routine or in the case of a fake borrower or benami loan or willful  defaulter or of a Company formed by so-called  entrepreneurs or where the debt would not be  serviceable from the income of the borrower or where the borrower has concealed their non-banking liability that can mislead the lender in ascertaining the net financial worth of the  borrower as well as the debt equity ratio and may  give rise to multiplicity of proceedings or where  the borrower has suppressed such other facts and  figures as are relevant for making the decisions by  the lenders. 

 12. I am of the view that, the entire facts and circumstances of this case, considered in their totality, justify giving the company an opportunity or chance to remain as a going concern by converting the EEF fund into loan, as proposed by the company/sponsors, at the rate of interest to be fixed by Bangladesh Bank for similar nature of project and upon furnishing such securities and on such terms and conditions that the Bank may prescribe for other projects of the same kind, to be done through its agent bank. In which case, the directors or promoters must provide personal guarantee too. 

 13. However, it should also be made clear that, the prayer has not been considered simply because of the promoter's/director's obvious commitments to provide adequate security against conversion of the said equity fund into loan. It should also be made clear that, in all appropriate cases, the first consideration should be to examine if there is any practical certainty i.e. the commercial feasibility about the survival and growth of a defaulter company/borrower. If the answer is no. or the prospect of recovery is too  uncertain then the court should consider the  petition for winding up. 

 14. However, in any case, no dishonest or non-compliant business concern or entity or businessman, who has or have managed to obtain loan by deceiving the bank or by suppressing their non-banking liabilities of substantial amount and have misled the lenders in ascertaining their actual net worth or in ascertaining the correct debt equity ratio or in rating their credit wortbines (credit rating). shall be given any indulgence by the lenders. Besides, it has to be noted here that, the fact of non-disclosure of non-banking liability can lead to multiplicity of proceedings, which constitutes a high risk factor, but has not yet been taken up by the bankers with the amount of concern that it practically deserve. 

 16. Besides, I am of the further opinion that, conversion of equity into loan, in a fit case, would make available the forum established under the Artha Rin (Loan Recovery) Act, 2003, to the equity partners, being distinct from lenders. 

 (B) The Bangladesh Bank is directed to consider the sponsor's application dated 10-10-2017, already filed to them, within 60 working days of receiving copy of this judgment and order and to convert the amount of equity investment of Taka 3.40 crore into principal loan to be sanctioned and treated through MIDAS. Bangladesh Bank shall fix such rate of interest for this loan as are fixed for similar nature of projects, while the interest should be charged and calculated from the date of disbursement of the equity fund and shall obtain as usual collateral and other securities, including personal guarantees of directors (and mortgage on their personal properties, if be required). Bangladesh Bank should ensure equitable treatment to the sponsors so far as the terms and conditions of the loan would be concerned, with liberty (of Bangladesh Bank) to reject the same and to refuse the conversion, if the terms and conditions to be prescribed by Bangladesh Bank, keeping parity in granting loan to similar business, are not accepted and proper security is not provided and if the respondent company cannot meet Bangladesh Bank's or loan sanctioning Bank's requirements within the time (to be not less than 60 working days from issuing the sanction letter) to be fixed by it, in which case the company shall stand wound up, upon expiry of the said period and the petitioner shall apply to this Court for appointment of Liquidator.
